<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Frederica S. Wilson, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Jahana Hayes>: H.R. 6502 creates several defined metrics related to a student's estimated net price, aimed at helping students understand how much they may pay for college after accounting for grants and scholarships. However, the bill's multiple net price definitions will make it very confusing for prospective students to actually estimate their cost of attendance. Specifically, the bill defines the following new terms: total net price required for completion; annual net price required for completion; total net price of attendance; and annual net price of attendance. None of these net price estimates paint a full picture of cost of attendance beyond tuition and fees.
The bill defines total net price required for completion as the difference between required costs charged a student and the amount of grant aid available to the student. By using this definition, students are only able to estimate how much they will pay for tuition and fees, and, if mandated by their institution, on-campus housing and dining services fees. This means that students who plan on living on campus will be unable to fully evaluate an adequate net price for institutions that offer, but do not require, on-campus housing or meal plans. But the bill also defines total net price of attendance, calculated as the sum of the total net price required for completion and indirect costs. As defined in H.R. 6502, the net price of completion metric does not adequately take into consideration ``indirect costs'' that arise for college students, which calls into question its value for students. Indirect costs include necessities such as transportation, housing, technology, and other costs, all of which students must bear to fully access and complete their coursework.\18\ For example, without having funds to access stable housing as they matriculate, a student cannot be expected to adequately tend to their studies. Therefore, the total net price required for completion metric does not paint the full picture of cost of attendance and its inclusion makes it harder for students to make ``apples-to-apples'' comparisons between various colleges.
\18\Planning for Indirect Costs, uAspire (last visited Jan. 5, 2026), https://www.uaspire.org/getattachment/57ed37ef-7ea9-4521-8c41- 39f4494e169c/FY25-Planning-for-Indirect- Expenses.pdf?lang=en-US.
A stronger metric to incorporate in the bill for purposes of the calculations of net price for completion would be the cost of attendance. The cost of attendance is typically known as the full price to attend an institution that more seamlessly incorporates both direct costs and indirect costs. In a 2022 report, the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that most colleges and universities do not provide students with all the information necessary to help students clearly understand their financial aid offers.\19\ GAO reported that approximately 55 percent of institutions do not provide a total cost of attendance that include key direct and indirect costs for students.\20\ GAO also found that an estimated 91 percent of institutions do not include or understate the net price, including both direct and indirect costs,\21\ in their financial aid offers.\22\ As a result of these findings, GAO recommended federal lawmakers to take up legislation to mandate institutions of higher education to follow best practices for providing students with clear and standard financial aid offers. Thus, to improve the financial aid offer letters, Congress must include better information on indirect costs and incorporate these costs into the standardized components of aid offer letters. Specifically, Committee Democrats strongly suggest defining any definition of ``net price'' as one that shows the difference between the cost of attendance and grant aid and requiring the consumer testing of all definitions that will be presented to students on an aid offer letter to determine if they provide clarity.
\19\U.S. Gov't Accountability Off., GAO-23-104708, Financial Aid Offers: Action Needed to Improve Information on College Costs and Student Aid (Nov. 2022), https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-23-104708.pdf.
\20\Id. GAO defined direct costs as ``Costs that are typically billed directly by the college. Examples include tuition, fees, and on-campus housing and meals.'' It defined indirect costs as ``Costs that students pay to other parties throughout the academic term. Examples include books, academic supplies, off-campus housing and meals, and other miscellaneous expenses, such as transportation.''.
\21\GAO defined net price as ``The actual amount a student will need to pay to attend a particular college. This should be estimated by subtracting gift aid (and not loans or work-study) from the full cost of attendance (key direct and indirect costs)''.
\22\Id.
Based on the limited standardization between offers mandated in this bill, and the proliferation of metrics that could inhibit students and families from making informed decisions, Committee Democrats recommend that H.R. 6502 integrate language from the Understanding the True Cost of College Act\23\, as it was incorporated into the College Cost Reduction Act\24\ last Congress. This would improve transparency and comparability by requiring a uniform format for financial aid offers with consistent terminology and a clear presentation of key cost components. Replacing the formatting requirements under H.R. 6502 and integrating the standards found in Understanding the True Cost of College Act and the College Cost Reduction Act that would fully standardize aid offers, helping students and families effectively compare aid offers and make better informed decisions about college costs.
\23\H.R. 3153, 119th Cong., (2025) https://www.congress.gov/bill/ 119th-congress/house-bill/3153.
\24\H.R. 6951, Sec. 111, 118th Cong., (2024) https:// www.congress.gov/118/bills/hr6951/BILLS-118hr6951rh.pdf.
PROGRAM-LEVEL METRICS ARE BEYOND THE SCOPE OF
FINANCIAL AID OFFERS
The program-level metrics required in financial aid offers by H.R. 6502, such as the average net price of attendance and the average net price of completion, go beyond what is necessary for helping students and families understand financial aid offers. Though Committee Democrats recognize that program-level metrics are important for students to have, adding this information on financial aid offers can create more confusion to helping students understand their aid offer and could make it more difficult to compare with other aid offers. Additionally, adding multiple program-level metrics could further complicate students' and families' ability to understand actual college costs and increase the risk of misinterpretation of the aid offer by students and families. Given that first-generation and low-income students typically face the greatest challenges navigating aid offers,\25\ this confusion could have the most significant impact on these student populations.
\25\U.S. Gov't Accountability Off., GAO-23-104708, FINANCIAL AID OFFERS Action Needed to Improve Information on College Costs and Student Aid 34, (2022) https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-23-104708.pdf.
H.R. 6502 REQUIREMENTS ON PRIVATE STUDENT LOANS WOULD BE DIFFICULT TO
IMPLEMENT
As drafted, H.R. 6502 requires institutions to provide detailed information in financial aid offer letters about private loans for which the student is ``eligible'', including details about each loan's interest rate, applicable fees, and repayment. Implementing the private student loan requirements of the bill may prove burdensome or unworkable for many institutions. Unlike federal student loans, private student lenders typically utilize a risk-based underwriting process to assess a prospective borrower's eligibility for a loan and the loan's terms. Determining this information for each student and each private lender would require institutions to work with all private lenders offering student loans to determine whether the terms of each loan apply to each individual student just to so the school could comply with the law. Finally, including private student loans with federal loans in aid offers, could further confuse students and parents unfamiliar with higher education financing. Committee Democrats urge Committee Republicans to omit provisions related to private student loans in the bill.
H.R. 6502 WOULD BE DIFFICULT TO IMPLEMENT WITH A GUTTED DEPARTMENT OF
EDUCATION
Since returning to office in January, the Trump Administration has made no secret of its plans to dismantle the Department of Education (Department) and in turn, has fired a significant number of staff.\26\ Shortly after being confirmed by the Senate, Secretary Linda McMahon initiated a reduction in force for the Department's staff, which impacted approximately 50 percent of the staff,\27\ who were experts in the policies and programs of the Department of Education, such as those at Federal Student Aid. Since that time the Department has attempted to fire even more staff. For instance, during the government shutdown in the fall, the Administration attempted to cut 465 Department employees, though they were later challenged in courts and ultimately stopped by Congress.\28\ Further, the Department has signed several interagency agreements to hand off much of its responsibilities to other agencies,\29\ with apparent plans to implement even more.\30\ Given the limited staff and H.R. 6502's requirements for the Department to develop, conduct and finalize financial aid offer requirements by July 1, 2028, Committee Democrats have very serious concerns about the Department's capacity to successfully implement this bill.

DEMOCRATIC AMENDMENTS OFFERED DURING MARKUP OF H.R. 6502
Committee Democrats put forward three amendments to improve the bill. One amendment would have replaced the text of H.R. 6502 with the text of H.R. 3153, the Understanding the True Cost of College Act. Two other amendments would prohibit the Secretary from handing off responsibilities to implement this bill either through transfers of authority or via interagency agreements. Committee Republicans rejected all the Democratic amendments that were considered.
